questions.prompt: A plugin provides llm, then starts a timer that calls the adapter. When the plugin stops, which disposer runs first?
options: The one that removes llm, because it was registered first
Both at once, because they belong to one fiber
The timer's, because disposers run in reverse order
questions.explanation: The fiber runs disposers from the last registration to the first. The timer stops before llm leaves the store, so no tick finds the adapter missing.

questions.prompt: Why does the kernel's plugin method register an effect that disposes the child fiber?
options: So the child plugin stops when the plugin that mounted it stops
So the child can read its parent's services
questions.explanation: The child's disposer goes on the parent's list. Disposing the parent therefore disposes the child too, and nothing stays running by accident.

questions.prompt: In dsh, two teardown steps are async and must run one after the other. What does the Cordis tutorial advise?
options: Register them as two separate effects in the right order
Put both steps in one disposer and await them there
Call the disposers yourself before unloading
Mark the second effect as prepend
questions.explanation: Cordis starts disposers in reverse order but awaits async ones together, so two effects can overlap. One disposer that awaits both steps keeps them in sequence.
